Special presentations: teal, chandelle, looper and dropping targets

The presentations in this lesson are about height and curve rather than angle. Their names are words used by course setters (the people who set up the traps), not rulebook terms. The rules list target types, and the Compak® Sporting rules ask for a variety of flights: rising, dropping and high, looping ones.

A teal (also springing or rising teal, named after the small duck) is thrown almost straight up: it slows, hangs still for a moment at the top and falls back. Shoot it either on the way up, moving the gun up through it from below, or at the top while it hangs. A common mistake is to stop the gun and jab at it while it hangs at the top. Some course setters use “springing” for a target that climbs at an angle rather than straight up, like a bird startled out of the grass.

A chandelle (French for “candle”) rises steeply on a slight curve, arcs over and drops almost vertically. Many shooters find it easiest to hit on the way up. Once it curls over and starts to fall, shoot in front of it (on the side it is moving towards) and below it.

A looper flies a wide arc across the sky, like a rainbow: it climbs, rolls over the top and falls. It is usually a standard target; some course setters also throw a battue on such a line, and it then shows its face as it turns. Follow the curve with the gun, staying ahead of the target and below it.

A dropping target is any target in the falling part of its flight. Because it is moving down as well as along, shoot below it and in front of it, with the gun moving.

Tip: Careful: names vary between countries. Many French speakers use “chandelle” for a target that goes almost straight up, which an English coach calls a teal. In other languages a word for “candle” may mean either. Whenever you hear chandelle or candle, ask: straight up or arcing over?

Key points

  • Teal: almost vertical up, stalls, falls; take it rising or at the peak.
  • Chandelle: steep curving climb, arcs over, drops almost vertically.
  • Looper: wide rainbow arc across, usually a standard target that rolls over the top and falls.
  • Dropping: lead underneath and in front; keep the gun moving.
  • Names vary: French speakers often say “chandelle” for a teal, so ask what is meant.

Did you know?

The French word chandelle means “candle”; it is also the name of an aerobatic manoeuvre in which a plane climbs steeply while turning.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Take the teal on the way up — keep the barrels moving above it.

    Meaning: Break the rising teal before the peak; the gun keeps rising past it.

  • Coach Don't poke at it on the top.

    Meaning: Do not stop and aim at the target while it stalls at the peak.

  • Coach The looper's turning over — underneath and in front.

    Meaning: The target is rolling over the top of its arc and starting to fall; the lead goes below and ahead of it.

  • Coach Second bird's dropping — go under it and keep the gun moving.

    Meaning: The second target of the pair is falling; shoot below it with the gun in motion.

  • Trajectory
  • Teal

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which target is thrown almost straight up, stalls at the top and falls back?

    1. Looper
    2. Quartering away
    3. Rabbit
    4. Teal
    Answer

    Teal

    That is the teal (springing or rising teal). A looper flies a wide arc across the sky.

  2. Where does the lead usually go on a dropping target?

    1. Above and behind
    2. Underneath and in front
    3. Straight at the target
    4. Only to the side, not down
    Answer

    Underneath and in front

    A falling target moves down as well as along, so part of the lead is vertical: below and ahead.

  3. A French-speaking coach says “chandelle”. What is the safest thing to do?

    1. Check: straight up, or an arc over the top?
    2. Assume it is a looper
    3. Assume it is a teal
    4. Ignore it, since it is not a rulebook term
    Answer

    Check: straight up, or an arc over the top?

    French speakers often mean an almost vertical target (an English teal), while an English setter’s chandelle climbs on a curve and arcs over; a quick check avoids a wrong plan.
